title: Even the wise drift (1 Kings 11:1–13)
hook: Solomon's heart turns in old age
carry: one small choice at a time

segments.voice: Yesterday, a queen came with riddles, chidot. Your line was the half was not told. Did you go and see something for yourself? Today, the end of Solomon's story, and it turns. Day seven hundred sixty-three.

A heart that hears. That's what Solomon asked for in a dream, at the very start. Since then he has judged between two mothers. He has built a house in quiet. He has prayed, saying heaven itself can't hold God, and asked that strangers be heard. A queen came to test him and went home amazed. Then the text turns a page and writes a sentence that begins, when Solomon was old. Nothing in it happens in a day. There's no single scene of falling. It's slower than that. Today's word is about slow.
screen: `A HEART THAT HEARS.` → `JUDGE, BUILDER, PRAYER.` → `WHEN SOLOMON WAS OLD.`

segments.voice: First Kings eleven. The text says Solomon loved many foreign women, and it gives the number itself: seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines. The Torah had warned that a king must not multiply wives, so that his heart not turn away. And verse four says just that, in the 1917 Jewish translation: "when Solomon was old, that his wives turned away his heart after other gods." He built high places for the gods of his wives' peoples, on the hill before Jerusalem. But the text doesn't let this be anyone else's fault. In the next verses, the LORD is angry with Solomon, because his heart was turned. His heart, the verse goes on, was not whole, in Hebrew not shalem, with God, as David's heart had been. The Talmud tells that Solomon reasoned he could take many wives and not be turned, and he was. Here's the word that matters: heart. Solomon's story opens with a heart, lev shomea, a listening heart. It closes with a heart that turned. Same heart. And the text gives no single moment when it turned. It lists marriages, then shrines for the gods of his wives, one after another. Nobody in the story wakes up one morning a different person. Many readers take Solomon's drift as a warning. The story doesn't call wisdom worthless. It shows that wisdom alone didn't keep him from turning. A king given wisdom in a dream still needed to keep choosing, every year, into old age. And the cost comes due in the next generation.
screen: `THE TORAH'S WARNING TO KINGS.` · `HIS HEART WAS NOT SHALEM.` · `A LISTENING HEART THAT TURNED.` · `ONE SMALL CHOICE, THEN ANOTHER.` · then, large: `WHEN SOLOMON WAS OLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: guard against slow drift. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something that matters to you that has slowly slipped: a habit of prayer or reflection, a friendship you used to tend, a promise to yourself, a value you once held tightly. No scolding. Just trace it back. Was there one small choice where the drift started? Breathe there. Then name one small choice that could turn you back toward it this week. If you pray, you can ask for a whole heart. The bell holds the time.
Shalem. The Hebrew word for whole, the wholeness Solomon's heart lost toward God as he grew old. Today's word.

Your line: one small choice at a time. Today, turn one thing you've let slip back by a single step. And look back at this week: a listening heart, the real mother gives way, finished before anyone hears it, a place to turn toward, hear the stranger too, the half was not told, and one small choice at a time. Day seven hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Jews read Solomon's later years in the book of Kings, and the Talmud uses his story to show why the Torah's limits on a king matter even for the wise.

fork.reveal: the Talmud tells that Solomon reasoned he could take many wives and not be turned, and the text says that when he was old, his heart was turned.

original.note: Hebrew: whole, complete. Solomon's heart was not shalem with God.

trapdoor: what you thought: Solomon was wise, so he stayed good.
what it means: the king who asked for a listening heart drifted slowly in old age.
what a scholar hears: the Torah's warning in Deuteronomy 17 uses the same picture: lest his heart turn away.

sources.quoted: when Solomon was old, that his wives turned away his heart after other gods

notes: The numbers (seven hundred wives, three hundred concubines) are stated in 1 Kings 11:3 and attributed to the text.
Sanhedrin 21b: Solomon said 'I will multiply and not turn aside', and turned. Confirm the citation.
The story must not read as blaming foreign women; the teach stresses the text's judgment falls on Solomon (11:9). Keeper to check tone.
